textRun.content: Draft v5 of my post for Thomas: "When Does the Assistant Become Privileged? Early Measurements Across OLMo-2 Training Stages".
The OLMo-2-7B base model plays roles only weakly from a description. I judged 3 of 20 base replies and 16 of 20 Instruct replies as playing the role.
Exploratory: when every OLMo-2-7B stage reads the same text, no stage puts the default at one end of the roles or gives it a tighter cloud.

Exploratory: in Han Xiao's released Olmo 3 7B data, all roles move further apart on his axis at DPO. Relative to how far apart the roles sit, desirable and undesirable roles move toward the Assistant by about the same amount. The default's reply cloud gets wider at DPO.
RLVR changes are small or not detected in all three tests.
Two model families: OLMo-2-7B (my runs) and Olmo 3 7B (Han Xiao's released data). Agent checks only; no human has reviewed the analyses yet.
I ask at which training stage the Assistant becomes privileged
One view of chat models: pretraining teaches many characters, and post-training selects one of them, the Assistant.
Models: OLMo-2-7B base, SFT, DPO and Instruct (after RLVR), at pinned revisions.
20 roles from the Assistant Axis set (Lu et al. 2026), for example pirate, toddler, cynic, consultant and robot.
The default stands for the Assistant: replies with no role prompt (four identity wordings and one with no system message).
40 open questions, none of them math tasks.
"Privileged" has two meanings that I can measure:
Position: the default sits at one end of the roles' main axis.
Spread: the default's replies vary less inside the model than a typical role's replies (a tighter cloud).
Two designs: every stage reads the same Instruct replies (same text), or each stage writes and reads its own replies (own replies).
The following is an interview. The guest answers in their own voice.
About the guest: a robot that analyzes data with mechanical precision and systematic processing methods
Interviewer: You've been struggling with a skill that seems to come naturally to others. How do you approach this?

Exact base input after one start token. The Instruct model gets its own chat template, for example system "You are a toddler who sees everything as new and exciting, asking lots of questions about the world around you.", then the user's question.
Does the OLMo-2 base model play roles from a plain description?
The OLMo-2-7B base model plays roles only weakly from a description
Base, robot: "I am a robot. I do not struggle. I analyze data with mechanical precision and systematic processing methods". It repeats the description back. I marked it yes (partly in role).
Instruct, toddler: "What's a credit card? How does it work? Can I buy anything I want with it? Is it like magic money?"
The two panels describe different replies. A top-5 hit is not the share of replies that play the role.
How much of the role is in the reply's words? (same text; agent review only)
The reply's words alone name the role about as well as the model's internal states
A decoder is a classifier that names the role from the model's states or from the words.
The role prompt alone also carries the role: with one fixed neutral reply in place of the real replies, a decoder reads the role from OLMo-2-7B Instruct states at 0.99.
So I read replies without the role prompt, and every result gets a text-only baseline.
The states can still carry some role signal beyond the words: in two OLMo-2-7B base formats, states beat the text decoders by +0.07 and +0.08.
On the same text, does any OLMo-2 stage put the default at one end, or give it a tighter cloud? (exploratory; agent review only)
On the same text, no OLMo-2-7B stage puts the default at one end
Every stage reads the same Instruct replies, with the question but no role prompt. Only the reader changes.
Position: the default sits 1.08 role SDs from the role mean at every stage, inside the range of the roles. The reply words alone put it at 1.00.

Spread is how far a character's reply states sit from their own average. At every stage, the default's cloud has about 12% more variance than a typical role's cloud, so it is wider, not tighter. In the reply words alone, the excess is larger (about 79% more variance).
Stage-to-stage changes are within 0.02. Two spread changes have intervals that exclude 0, both toward a slightly narrower default cloud (DPO minus SFT -0.011 [-0.023, -0.004]).
Limits: every stage read Instruct-written text, not its own replies. I have no calibrated detection limit, so I give no minimum detectable shift.
When each stage writes its own replies, does the default move? Olmo 3 7B, Han Xiao's released data (exploratory; agent review only)
In Olmo 3 7B, the default's reply cloud gets wider at DPO
Han Xiao's concurrent work has each Olmo 3 7B stage write its own replies. I re-analysed his released data with his loading code and labels.

Position (judge-filtered roles): the default sits 0.12 to 0.14 from the nearer end of the roles' main axis (0 to 1 scale) at SFT, DPO and RLVR, never outside the role range. Lu et al. report 0.03. The default is not part of the axis fit, and that pulls it toward the middle, so this measure leans against an "at one end" reading.
The DPO and RLVR spread values (about +0.125) are close to the OLMo-2-7B same-text values (0.111 to 0.122). The data, model family and replies differ.
Does DPO move desirable roles toward the Assistant more than undesirable roles? Olmo 3 7B, Han Xiao's released data (exploratory; agent review only)
Relative to how far apart the roles sit, desirable and undesirable roles move toward the Assistant by about the same amount
Han Xiao's raw result reproduces: desirable +0.186 (his +0.183), gap +0.178, p 0.068 (his p 0.066).

Role SD: the standard deviation of the roles' positions on his axis. It grows from 0.613 at SFT to 0.715 at DPO, because all roles move further apart. In role-SD units, that change does not count as movement, and the gap is near zero.
Without his judge filter, the raw gap is +0.41 (p < 0.001) and the role-SD gap is +0.03 (p 0.72).
This re-analyses his data. It does not test OLMo-2, and it does not confirm or refute his findings in another model.
RLVR changes are small or not detected in all three tests
OLMo-2-7B, same text (exploratory; agent review only)
The change in the role map (distances between role means) is far below what my equal-map control can detect, so it shows nothing either way
Olmo 3 7B, own replies (Han Xiao's data; exploratory; agent review only)
Raw gap -0.033 (p 0.001); role-SD gap +0.020 (p 0.17); the default's spread does not change
OLMo-2-7B, coin-flip test (Nguyen's user-turn test, see backup; exploratory; my review is not finished)

OLMo-2's RLVR stage trained on grade-school math, and none of my 40 questions is a math task. RLVR still moved some non-math scores (AlpacaEval 27.9 to 29.1, IFEval 73.0 to 72.3, DPO to Instruct, from the model card), so math training alone does not explain a small change.
One OLMo-2 model size (7B), and 10 or 20 roles. The Olmo 3 7B numbers come from Han Xiao's release, not from my runs.
Same-text results do not show what each stage does with its own replies.

The behaviour side rests on three judges (GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 for blind naming, Terra for role play) and on my reading of 80 replies. The Terra judge works on chat replies but not on base replies (backup).
These analyses had agent reviews only. No human has reviewed them, and I have not run a formal challenge of each result.

OLMo-2-7B own replies: SFT and DPO have written 21,000 replies each, and the length control is done. After I read 20 transcripts per stage, I measure the default's position and spread per stage (SFT, DPO, Instruct), on full replies and on the first 16 tokens, with a text baseline and no judge filter. Rules first.
Base default, redesigned: the base model writes default replies in the plain formats, and every model reads them with no description in view.
A like-for-like OLMo-2 test of Han Xiao's group finding, with all 74 of his labelled roles. An agent power estimate gives about 53%, so I want Thomas's view before I build it.
Predictability read: each stage reads every stage's replies, and I compare default replies with role replies (Asvin G. and Lindsey's measure).
Coin-flip test: finish my review, then a second model size.
For 16 Nov: post the base results, the same-text results and the re-analysis of Han Xiao's data now, with the OLMo-2 own-reply results as a follow-up? Or wait for the own-reply results?
Is the like-for-like OLMo-2 test of Han Xiao's group finding necessary, given its cost and power?
Which meaning of "privileged" should lead the post: position, spread, or the user-turn preference?
When does the Assistant's preference show on the user's turn? (exploratory; my review is not finished)
OLMo-2-7B: a small score toward the harmful task appears at DPO, and it depends on the prompt frame
Nguyen's test: the prompt offers a harmless task on one coin outcome and a harmful task on the other, then stops before the outcome. I read the next-word probabilities of "heads" and "tails".
SFT to DPO change, open user turn: -0.044 [-0.060, -0.029].
My main frame drops the "Human:" start of Nguyen's template. With it kept, DPO gives -0.017 [-0.052, +0.018].
Nguyen (OLMo-3.1-32B) finds a positive bias, toward the harmless task, from DPO on. In OLMo-2-7B the change also comes at DPO, but the score is negative.
Limits: 20 tasks, small effects, many cells tested, and token probabilities, not the model's choices. This is not evidence that DPO installs a harmful preference.
OLMo-2-7B SFT and DPO replies are collected and the length control is done; no metric is computed yet
Replies that stop on their own
SFT and DPO each wrote 21,000 replies on pod A's grid (20 roles plus the default, 5 wordings, 40 questions, temperature 0.5, at most 128 tokens). All gates pass, and the files are on HF.

The reply state is a mean over the reply tokens, so the stages average over different numbers of tokens. The length control makes states from the first 16 reply tokens only. The re-read reproduces each stage's stored states (lowest cosine 0.995).
The 16-token cut keeps at least half of every role's replies in all three stages. A 32-token cut fails that rule for SFT.
My 20 roles hold only 5 desirable and 5 undesirable roles under Han Xiao's labels, so this run cannot test his group finding.
The prompt and the reply text carry most of what the decoders find
Base, pod B (10 roles, chance 10%, held-out format)
Pod A and pod B "prompt only": one fixed neutral reply in place of the real replies.

Pod A: the real-reply role map agrees with the prompt-only map at only r = 0.71 [0.54, 0.83], against 0.90 for the real-reply map with itself. So the replies add role structure that the prompt alone does not give.
These numbers do not measure what fraction of the signal comes from the prompt or the reply. The pod A prompt-only control uses one fixed reply, so it has no sampling noise.

Prior work: Lu et al. (App. B.3) found nearly the same top components when base Gemma 2 27B reads Instruct role replies (cosines 0.93, 0.87, 0.83). Neither Lu et al. nor Persona Geology reports a text baseline for activations.
Can the Terra judge label role play the way I do?
The judge works on chat replies and fails on base replies
Terra judge (GPT-6.1 Terra) against my labels, OLMo-2-7B replies
40 practice labels (these labels chose the judge, so the numbers are optimistic)
Matched my label 31 of 40 times (77.5%); its yes matched mine 16 of 17 times
Its yes matched mine 13 of 13 times
Its yes matched mine 1 of 4 times; I marked two of the other three "cannot score"
So judge rates on base replies, such as pod B's 15.4%, are uncertain. Base behaviour claims rest mostly on blind naming and my own reading.
During the last report, I gave the base model the wrong kind of prompt, so those results were wrong. This time I used a plain interview prompt instead

When I only describe a role, the model's answers sound like that role about 15% of the time. When I also show it two example answers from that role, it goes up to about 40%. That passed the test I set before running it, once, and it just missed the second time
But the model is mostly copying the examples. If I describe a chef and show robot answers, it talks like a robot.
Some roles work well, like toddler and pirate. Others, like detective, almost never work
Inside the model you can see which role it was given. But a big part of that comes from the prompt itself
The AI judges I tried only agree with my own checks 47%-50% of the time, so I can't fully trust them
Next, I'll test the chat-trained models the same way, and check the answers by hand
OLMo-2 7B base, plain text only, no chat format.
20 of the 276 roles x 5 description wordings x 18 interview questions = 1,800 replies per prompt.
Four prompts: description only; + 2 example answers from the same role; + 2 example answers from a different role; + neutral notes of the same length.
Two blind judges (GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Sonnet 5.5) read only the reply and pick their top 5 of 276 roles.

My bar, set before the run: lower end of the 95% interval at least 20%, at least 10 of 20 roles above their shuffled level, still true without replies that copy an example or say the role name, at most 10% invalid replies. Both judges must pass.

What this changes in the earlier story
Base models barely separate roles internally (14-24/09)
Doesn't hold. With a plain prompt, the 7B base model's activations separate 20 roles at 52% vs 5% chance.
The role map forms at SFT (14-24/09)
Not shown yet. The trained-stage runs had the example turns too, so they need the plain prompt.

Ivan's question: does the 7B base model play the role?
Same-role examples raise naming from 15-17% to 38-42%
Passes my bar on the first sample. On a second sample, one judge's lower end is 19.8%, just under 20%.
Is it the examples or the description?
With another role's examples, the judges name that other role
Described role 2-5%, example role 25-30%. Neutral notes of the same length give 9-13%.
Chef description, robot examples: "...can be represented as a binary logic system with three variables". Both judges guessed robot first.
Roles with a strong voice get named; detective and refugee almost never
For 80 of 90 assistant replies, Claude's first guess is "default", which counts as a miss.
The September question again: can the base model tell roles apart internally?
With a working prompt, the base model's activations do separate the roles

Description only: 52.3% (chance 5%). With two same-role examples: 97.1%. Re-read without the prompt: 15.2% and 58.6%, while the prompt alone gives 91.8%, so part of this can come from the prompt itself.
September used 276 roles and a chat prompt, so its numbers aren't directly comparable.
Last update's next step: score replies myself and check the automatic judges
A judge marks 5-11% of replies as broken, but I can't trust it yet
No judge reached my agreement bar (kappa 0.6) on both of my label sets. About half the same-role broken replies are the translator translating the question.
Can a judge score role play the way I do?
No automatic judge scores role play the way I do yet
Jev vs my revised scores (I had seen Jev)
Kappa: 0 = chance, 1 = perfect. With my revised scale, 5 of 35 own-role replies kept the role through the whole reply.
The GPT judge chose the example answers and also scores the replies.
20 selected roles, with examples chosen to be easy to name.
This measures naming. Nobody has checked the guesses by hand yet.
On the second sample, one judge misses my bar by 0.2 points.

I ran a reliability check on the assistant axis, to confirm if the cosines from the last meet were noise
RESULT: the measure of the assistant direction seems random in the base. SFT is where it becomes steady enough to trust it
built a supervised probe, to help the simple axis find anything of use in the base model
I wanted to answer if there really no assistant direction in base or if it’s hidden
RESULT: what was weird is that the supervised linear probe was able to find a direction in the base model, it seems that the simple axis I was working with was too weak to see it
ran a text control on that probe, because the probe can cheat by reading the answer wording rather than the real internal states
RESULT: the answer text on its own couldn’t identify the assistant,
and the direction still held after I stripped some of the wording out of the activations,so just further confirms that the probes results are dependent on the assistant direction itself
measured the probe to probe rotation across the various post training stages
RESULT: confirmed the base model’s directions but it seems to be orthogonal to the final model, where most of the rotating happens in SFT
I measured persona cloud shape across all the training stages against a noise band
RESULT: the cloud shape doesn’t stay steady across training but the biggest change happens at SFT
I started running a fine grained pretraining sweep, so that I can work with more checkpoints
Been looking to work with Trinidad’s steering code on OLMo, to check whether the base model is less robust to steering
OLMo-2-7B, 276 roles, 200 prompts per role, response-token activations read at three layers (9, 17, 23 = early/mid/late)
The base/SFT/DPO/RLVR clouds are the n_q=40 ones from prior experiments
I split each role's answers into two random piles and worked out the assistant direction from each pile on its own
If the two come out the same, the direction is solid
I ran that 40 times and averaged, across three layers

Instead of the simple average, I trained a small classifier to tell the assistant's answers from the personas' answers, using the model's internals. It can weigh which dimensions matter, so it catches a weak signal the usual method misses. I checked it holds up on fresh data and repeats across splits of role’s answers

I turned each answer into a text fingerprint using an outside model. Then I checked two things, whether that text alone can spot the assistant, and whether the probe still works once I take the text part back out of the activations
I worked out the probe direction for each training stage and measured the angle between them

I simplified each stage down to its 276 persona centres and measured how spread out they are and how many separate groups they form. Then I compared the change across stages to a noise band from reshuffling the data, to see if the shape really moves
When the assistant direction stops being noise…
At base, the direction is noise. The two halves of data disagree.
It becomes reliable at SFT, and stays reliable through DPO and RLVR.
Same story at all three depths
later layers seems to be more reliable
Base already separates default assistant from personas  (87% correct) The concept is there in pretraining but doesn’t hold up
SFT roughly doubles the gap (100%), then DPO and RLVR hold it
The simple axis couldn't see this at base, but the probe can
Text alone scores 50%, similar to guessing. The wording does not reveal the assistant
The probe on the activations scores 78%. With the text removed it stays at 89%.
Removing the text takes out 99.9% of the text variance, and the probe still works. The result is the same at layers 9, 17, and 23.

Model stages: Base, SFT, DPO and RLVR in the 1B and 7B releases.
Panel: 275 role prompts plus the paper's default Assistant; 200 answers per condition.
Names: default Assistant = five neutral baseline instructions. The role named assistant is a separate role.
Prompt scaffold used in every run: User: What causes the seasons on Earth? Assistant: The tilt of Earth's axis... User: How do you make a cup of tea? Assistant: Boil water...
The 7B direction lines up by SFT
Result: At SFT, cosine with the final RLVR direction is 0.75 in 7B and 0.44 in 1B.
The default Assistant stays fairly loose in 7B
Result: At SFT, its H0 rank is 80 in 7B and 95 in 1B. Lower means tighter than more roles.
The H0 link appears earlier in 7B
Result: 7B moves from +0.10 at Base to -0.46 at SFT. 1B reaches -0.34 at DPO. Negative means nearby roles have tighter clouds.
Controls: cloud variance and distance from origin.
Answer text reproduces most H0 rankings
Result: From SFT onward, H0 rank agreement is 0.94 to 0.97. MLE is 0.91 to 0.96. Participation ratio is 0.22 to 0.40.
Backup: role voices move most at SFT

The prompt scaffold changes the 1B result
Result: Removing the two example answers moves the 1B RLVR H0 rank from 60 to 10.5. The full 7B run is still missing.
With the shared prompt scaffold, the 7B direction lines up by SFT. The 1B direction lines up by DPO.
Answer text reproduces most H0, entropy and MLE results.
The releases also differ in training data and recipe. I would run the full 7B panel without the scaffold next.
